pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32937

This PR includes the necessary setup to generate the NuGet package for this project.

Once this is in, our CI will start to generate the preview package requested by the Blazor team.
cc @mkArtakMSFT @terrajobst
pr_comments:
Note regarding the `new-api-needs-documentation` label:

This serves as a reminder for when your PR is modifying a ref *.cs file and adding/modifying public APIs, to please make sure the API implementation in the src *.cs file is documented with triple slash comments, so the PR reviewers can sign off that change.
This hasn't been API reviewed yet, has it?
I thought this was API reviewed.  I know we've had a couple API review meetings and discussed it.  @terrajobst

Immo's comment on that issue suggests it hasn't:
"We did a brief run in a smaller group; at this point we should go ahead with the implementation first to see what issues we encounter and do the API review after with the complete API set and all modifications we made since then."
and the issue is still marked as being a suggestion rather than approved.

@stephentoub

> This hasn't been API reviewed yet, has it?

We did a feature crew review of the spec at some point, which has had many of the same people. I considered that enough to let the dev start. My goal was to do a final pass when we're further along. I didn't forsee that the Blazor teams needs a final version by Build (we only planned for a preview).

I'll set up an out-of-order for tomorrow.

@pranavkm Can you please take a look at `TranscodingReadStream` and `TranscodingWriteStream`? 
I removed dependency on netcoreapp APIs for all TFMs. Also tweaked a bit the implementation based on @stephentoub's feedback.
@stephentoub I think I already addressed all of the comments; is there anything else you want me to change?
CI issues seem to be unrelated.

I will proceed to merge this.

Next steps:
* Add suggestions for .NET 5-only on a subsequent PR.
* Port last commits (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/33459/commits/c4282f2e7e20c2a866db33b12e887e91d75b3e4e and beyond) to https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/tree/release/3.1-blazor.

issue_context.title: Add extension methods for HttpClient that allow serialization from/to JSON
issue_context.body:
The spec is here:

https://github.com/dotnet/designs/blob/main/accepted/2020/json-http-extensions/json-http-extentions.md

Related issues:

* https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/1754
* https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/31550
* https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/31551
comments: @terrajobst you linked 2x the same issue. Does it have to go through API review first?

From:  https://github.com/dotnet/designs/blob/master/accepted/2020/json-http-extensions/json-http-extentions.md

>Serializing and deserializing JSON payloads from the network is a very common operation for clients, especially in the upcoming Blazor environment. Right now, sending a JSON payload to the server requires multiple lines of code, which will be a major speed bump for those customers. We'd like to add extension methods on top of HttpClient that allows doing those operations with a single method call.

Why add these as extension methods to HttpClient? Why not just add them as regular methods to HttpClient?

@karelz 

> you linked 2x the same issue.

Clipboard is hard man! Fixed.

> Does it have to go through API review first?

We did a brief run in a smaller group; at this point we should go ahead with the implementation first to see what issues we encounter and do the API review after with the complete API set and all modifications we made since then.

@karelz 

I see you set the milestone to 5.0. Please note that we need to ship a preview by Build; it looks like we don't have a milestone for that. Should we?

@terrajobst unless we have more than 5-10 issues tracking as must have for Build, I don't think it makes sense to create milestone/label.
And once we hit the threshold, let's discuss what makes most sense ... (I feel that a label will be more flexible, but I may be wrong).

`JsonContent.Create(...)` usage is unlike other `HttpContent` we have. We should see if these could reasonably be changed to `new JsonContent(...)`.

The verbs are also inconsistent with current naming. Something to consider:
- `HttpClient.GetFromJsonAsync` vs `HttpClient.GetStringAsync`
- `HttpContent.ReadFromJsonAsync` vs `HttpContent.ReadAsStringAsync`

Otherwise I think these APIs look good. I used the Formatting assembly extensively in a past life and would have had no problems migrating to this.

> I want to propose having these methods throw an exception when the response status code is not 2xx

I would expect the convenience methods (the ones not returning `HttpResponseMessage`) to do exactly that.

> and to include the HttpResponse in that exception

`HttpRequestException` will include a `StatusCode` property in .NET 5. We will not be including the full response, as having an `IDisposable` inside an exception  is just asking for trouble.

Because I'm an idiot, I filed a new issue for today's API review (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/33566#issuecomment-598845161) instead of using this. I've marked this as API approved. I'll close the review one in favor of this.

> `JsonContent.Create(...)` usage is unlike other `HttpContent` we have. We should see if these could reasonably be changed to `new JsonContent(...)`.
> 
> The verbs are also inconsistent with current naming. Something to consider:
> 
>     * `HttpClient.GetFromJsonAsync` vs `HttpClient.GetStringAsync`
> 
>     * `HttpContent.ReadFromJsonAsync` vs `HttpContent.ReadAsStringAsync`

Seems like these comments weren't addressed even though this PR was merged?

review_comments: Couldn't the call sites for these methods just use JsonContent.Create instead of CreateJsonContent?
This test only validates that the `Content-Type` header contains the expected value, not that the raw data sent on the wire is indeed UTF-16. Is this intentional?
Why is this not supported?  This should be made to work.
(We should also override the other reading methods, like ReadByte, Read(Span), ReadAsync(Memory), Begin/EndRead, etc.)

Why do we need to implement them? This is an internal type and is implementation detail to only use the async methods (`ReadAsync`). Why do we need to implement something that we are not going to use.

If it's only used internally by JsonSerializer.DeserializeAsync, then it's fine.

Note that HttpClient is getting sync methods, though, so the sync methods on the write stream will be usable.
Can we do that on a follow-up PR that applies all the necessary changes that are only valid for .NET 5?

This stream is being potentially handed out to user code.  As with my comment the write stream should null these out, the read stream must as well; otherwise, user code using this stream after it's been disposed is going to lead to using a buffer that's already been returned to the pool.

cc: @GrabYourPitchforks
Can you elaborate, how is it possible to hand out `TranscodingReadStream` to user code? I will null out the arrays, though.
My comment is from before I understood that you were only handing it to the JsonSerializer.
Are these `Core` methods called outside of the above two? If not, why not merge them?
As per https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/33459#discussion_r393883547 suggests, I did it to make the validations outside of the `async` method.

This needs to Dispose the stream passed into the ctor.  Otherwise, it's going to potentially leak HTTP connections until the finalizer gets around to cleaning things up.

But per my half-complete comments in the release/3.1 PR, you need to be careful: when you make the change to this read stream, if you also make the change to the write stream, then when you dispose of the stream in SerializeToStreamAsync in order to return the rented buffers, you'd also end up disposing the underlying stream there, which you shouldn't do.

This is generally handled by having a leaveOpen bool argument to the decorator stream's constructor, where it indicates whether Dispose on the decorator should dispose or not dispose the underlying stream.
@pranavkm isn't this also missing from aspnet? or is the input stream being disposed somewhere else?
Not for now, but if the language ends up adding T?? for C# 9, we'll want to change the return type here to be `Task<TValue??>`.

I commented later in the implementation, but commenting here on the ref as well:
- Should we be consistent about ctor vs factory methods? e.g. should we make the ctors internal/private and add non-generic Create methods?
- As defined the implementation has no choice but to box a `T value`.  We could avoid that if we made `Value` virtual.
- Same value + type ordering question as above.

This could fail if *_charBuffer* is empty, *_encoder* contains some leftover state from the previous call, _flush = true_, and _readBuffer_ is too small to contain the transcoded result. At that point the `Convert` routine won't be able to make any forward progress at all, and it will throw.

The fix would be to make sure that the destination buffer to which `Convert` writes is always large enough to make at least some forward progress. I think using your overflow buffer would work well here.

Is there a reason you chose to use `ArraySegment<byte>` rather than `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`?  Note that JsonSerializer.Serialize ends up using the Stream.WriteAsync method that takes a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, so it'd be more efficient if this stream overrode that WriteAsync method and made it the primary workhorse... it can then override the byte[]-based version to just delegate to the memory-based one.
`WriteAsync(ReadOnlyMemory<Byte>, ...` is not available on NS2.0, but as per the Blazor team, they are fine with this package targeting NS2.1, is that change worth the upgrade?

For the OOB, it's probably not worth it.  But it is for the netcoreapp build:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/33459/files#diff-8d366f561ace3bceddbe061546d673f6R3
Using the memory-based overload here would be useful, too, and actually more so than with the write stream.
Where did the constant `4` come from?

This decision comes from https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/12142#discussion_r304970713.
EDIT: Disregard this comment, I didn't notice that the linked comment is talking about the `OverflowBuffer`, not the `MaxByteBufferSize`.

There should at minimum be a comment explaining why the constant was chosen. Keep in mind that the max chars-to-bytes expansion for UTF-8 is 3 (not 4) bytes per char. But clearly we're not transcoding _to_ UTF-8 (since the input was already UTF-8), so using any UTF-8 specific constant would not be correct.

It's perfectly ok if we say something like "this is a reasonable guess for a worst-case expansion for a typical encoding". But IMO there needs to be a comment that says _something_. :)

Done.
Added the following comment:
```
Upper bound that limits the byte buffer size to prevent an encoding that has a very poor worst-case scenario.
```

Now that makes me question if we should limit the char buffer on the Read side for the same reason.
Same question as earlier about using MaxCharBufferSize vs _charBuffer.Length.

Having a larger `byteBuffer` than the one expected should not have any negative impact, we only use it to buffer bytes transcoded to the target encoding; see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/33459/files#diff-f1d0073534d8aeb4e012aecd2149b958R127.


cc @pranavkm since he wrote this originally.
Write should be implemented, as should Begin/EndWrite, WriteByte, Write(Span), WriteAsync(ReadOnlyMemory), etc.

@ManickaP is currently implementing sync APIs for HttpClient (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/32125).  Once that's in place, these synchronous Write/Flush methods will become callable.  If we're not exposing this stream publicly, then technically we only need to implement the sync APIs that HttpClient itself will use, which means Write/Flush/etc.  You and she can work out whether it makes to do that in your PR or hers, but we should make sure it happens, otherwise this Content type will be broken.
Same commnet as here https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/33459#discussion_r395833435

The existing methods are named ReadAsStringAsync, ReadAsByteArrayAsync, ReadAsStreamAsync, etc.  It's strange that these are then "ReadFromJsonAsync".  Seems like they should instead be ReadAsJsonAsync, ReadAsJsonObjectAsync, ReadAsObjectAsync, ReadAsInstanceAsync, ReadAsTypeAsync, or something along those lines.
@GrabYourPitchforks, if you haven't already, can you review the encoding/decoding logic in these read/write streams?

As per the [spec](https://github.com/dotnet/designs/blob/master/accepted/2020/json-http-extensions/json-http-extentions.md#whats-the-behavior-of-content-type), we allow `application/json` and `text/plain` only.

If Content-Type is null we assume it as "application/octet-stream" in accordance with section 7.2.1 of the HTTP spec.
This is how Formatting API works as well.

And at the same time, it is contrary to how `HttpContent.ReadAsStringAsync` works (it allows null content-type and tries to read the content using UTF-8 for that case).

IMO, null Content-Type should default to `application/json; charset=utf-8`.

> And at the same time, it is contrary to how HttpContent.ReadAsStringAsync works (it allows null content-type and tries to read the content using UTF-8 for that case).

I know that JSON does have some rules about BOMs (I believe writing them is forbidden, reading them is left up to implementer?). We should make sure we're consistent with that.

The web is a pretty wild place 👍. There are specs but there are also lots of implementations that don't conform in subtle ways, so this is good advice (and similar to what we do on the server side with JSON). 

---

I would expect this to also support suffix content types. `application/<something>+json` - https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6839

In use by places like github: https://developer.github.com/v3/media/ - it's a newer spec, but lots of more [serious](https://github.com/cloudevents/spec) and large scale kinds of API design will prefer this over `application/json`. 

We might be able to get away with ignoring `text/json` which had some usage long ago, but isn't to spec.
I'm a little bit surprised about `text/plain`. I'm not sure I've seen that in use for JSON.

I can't remember why I put it in the spec; I think it was based on feedback of someone because I wouldn't have been smart enough to put either of these mime types in. If you believe `text/plain` is wrong let's remove it. Do we consider adding additional mime types in the future as a breaking change? IOW, would people commonly catch exceptions can do something different if a given mime type isn't accepted/produced by the server?

+1 on the support for suffix content type. As of now, you are unable to read [problem details responses](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7807) that MVC produces for error responses. It has a `application/problem+json` content type.

What I get from this is that we need to white-list the following:
* `application/json`
* `application/<something>+json`
* ~`text/plain`~

@rynowak @pranavkm Is that correct or is there any other Content-Type you want to add?
Sounds right to me.

Yup, this looks fine. ASP.NET Core has two implementations for calculating media-type subsets:

* https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/src/Mvc/Mvc.Core/src/Formatters/MediaType.cs#L286-L291
* https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/src/Http/Headers/src/MediaTypeHeaderValue.cs#L385-L396

The first has fewer code dependencies and might be easier to easier to copy to S.T.Json if you'd like to use it as an implementation.
